issues.subcategory: inconsistent count of critical details
issues.description: The number of critical details is reported inconsistently across the manuscript. The Materials section states there are eight critical details in the movie, but the collaborative recognition test is said to refer to only four critical details (with eight control questions). The individual memory test then covers 'eight... critical details included in the movie.' This creates confusion about how many discrepant items exist, how many are discussed, and how the within-subjects comparison (discussed vs. non-discussed) is constructed. If there are 8 critical details and 4 are discussed, this should be stated consistently; the design's counterbalancing and analysis depend on these numbers being clear.
issues.quote: Both versions are identical except for eight critical details... The test will comprise 12 questions, four of which refer to critical details (e.g., What color was Eric’s cap?), with the other eight being control questions... The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie

issues.subcategory: improbable/implausible correlation value used in power analysis
issues.description: The power analyses rely on an assumed correlation of r = 0.07 between the discussed and non-discussed (repeated) measures. This is an extraordinarily low correlation for two memory accuracy measures derived from the same individuals, and it is not justified. The correlation between repeated measures has a substantial effect on required sample size for within-between interaction power analyses. Relying on a single, very low, possibly aggregated/idiosyncratic value without justification or sensitivity analysis undermines the validity of all reported sample size requirements.
issues.quote: The joint correlation of results in the discussed and non-discussed items in both studies available was 0.07.

issues.subcategory: questionable pooling of heterogeneous effect sizes
issues.description: The two studies used to estimate the memory conformity effect size for the replication power analysis have wildly different effect sizes (Hedges' g = 1.92 vs g = 0.38), differing by a factor of ~5. Pooling these via random effects yields a 'joint' g = 1.13, but the enormous heterogeneity makes this pooled estimate nearly meaningless for planning. The required sample of 18 derived from this is likely a substantial underestimate if the true effect is closer to the lower study. The heterogeneity itself should preclude treating the pooled value as a reliable basis for power.
issues.quote: The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges’ g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges’ g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020).... random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13.

issues.subcategory: unit of analysis problem
issues.description: Participants are run in pairs and engage in collaborative recall together; the misinformation each receives is determined by their partner's responses during a shared discussion. Responses within a pair are therefore non-independent, yet the analysis plan treats participants as independent units in ANOVA (240 participants / 120 pairs). Failure to account for the nested (dyadic) structure inflates effective sample size and risks Type I error. No multilevel/dyadic modeling is proposed.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs).... The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels

issues.subcategory: differential/selective attrition through exclusion replacement
issues.description: Participants who correctly guess the hypotheses will be excluded and replaced. The authors themselves acknowledge this will likely produce more exclusions in the experimental groups than in the control group, because the interventions (warning, education, demonstration) make the deception salient. This differential exclusion threatens the comparability of groups (selecting out the most suspicious/insightful participants disproportionately from treatment groups), potentially biasing estimates of intervention efficacy. Replacement to maintain n does not solve the selection bias.
issues.quote: If any of the participants correctly guesses our hypotheses, they will be excluded from the analysis and replaced with another person in order to maintain the correct sample size. We realize that this may result in more exclusion in the three experimental groups than in the control group

issues.subcategory: underspecified primary outcome among multiple indices
issues.description: Four indices are derived from the individual memory test (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total number of answers), and multiple analyses (accuracy on filler/non-discussed/discussed, disputed vs non-disputed coding) are planned, but no single primary dependent variable for the key efficacy test is designated, nor is correction for multiple comparisons specified. Because the dependent variable used for the within-between interaction is not pinned down, there is substantial researcher degrees of freedom in selecting which index yields the desired interaction. In a Registered Report this should be locked down.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.subcategory: operationalization change from forced-choice to open-ended without validation
issues.description: Prior MORI research and the replication target (Garry et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2019) used two-alternative forced-choice tests, where 'misinformation-consistent' has a precise meaning. The authors switch to open-ended questions and redefine what counts as misleading. This change alters the measurement of the core construct (memory conformity), affecting base rates, guessing, and comparability with the literature the study claims to replicate. The effect-size estimates used for power were derived from forced-choice designs and may not transfer to an open-ended measure, undermining both the replication claim and the power analysis.
issues.quote: First we will examine the memory conformity effect using the procedure of Garry et al. (2008; also Ito et al., 2019), but with modification concerning applying open-ended questions in the individual memory test.

issues.subcategory: confounded multi-component interventions
issues.description: Two of the three interventions are bundles of multiple components (e.g., Demonstration and motivation = DRM demonstration + motivational podcast; Extended warning = several distinct messages including enlightenment, source-monitoring info, confidence message). Because components are confounded within each condition, any observed effect cannot be attributed to a specific mechanism, limiting the theoretical/practical conclusions the design can support. The authors acknowledge overlap but do not design to disentangle it.
issues.quote: we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.subcategory: non-equivalent control condition / dosage confound
issues.description: The interventions differ from the control not only in content but in modality and engagement: experimental groups receive memory-relevant podcasts and (for DRM) an active task with personalized feedback, whereas the control receives a podcast on 'soft skills related to social attitudes.' The Demonstration and motivation group in particular involves active task engagement and personalized feedback absent from other conditions, confounding intervention content with task engagement/attention. This makes it impossible to isolate whether effects are due to memory-specific content versus general engagement/attention.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: label/content mismatch in procedure description
issues.description: In the Procedure section, the 'Extended warning' group is described as listening to a podcast about 'memory functioning and its imperfections,' while the 'Education about memory' group listens to a podcast about 'the functioning and sins of memory.' These descriptions are nearly identical and blur the distinction between the two conditions, contradicting the Materials section which describes the Extended warning podcast as focused on the misinformation effect, source misattribution, confidence, and enlightenment about the deception. This inconsistency makes it unclear what each group actually receives.
issues.quote: Participants in the ‘Extended warning’ group will listen to the podcast about ‘memory functioning and its imperfections’; those in in the ‘Education about memory’ group will listen to the podcast about the functioning and sins of memory.

issues.subcategory: missing details on DRM lure feedback and predefined lures
issues.description: The DRM debriefing script names specific critical lures ('doctor, window, sweet, thief') and states four lists will be chosen that produce the strongest effect 'on the basis of our previous research,' but no data, list contents, or selection criteria are provided. Because the demonstration's persuasive power (and thus the intervention's efficacy) depends on participants actually falsely recalling lures, and because this is given as personalized feedback regardless of whether each participant actually produced the lure, the manuscript lacks detail needed to evaluate whether the feedback will be accurate/valid for each participant.
issues.quote: See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief. If so, you were fooled.... Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect.

issues.subcategory: restricted age sample and lab setting overgeneralization
issues.description: The sample is restricted to 16–35-year-olds recruited via media/internet advertisements, yet the introduction repeatedly frames implications for 'the proper functioning of justice systems' and real-world witness interrogation. The narrow age range, self-selected convenience sample, and laboratory paradigm limit generalizability to the broader population of real eyewitnesses (including older adults, children, and forensically realistic contexts), which is not adequately acknowledged as a limitation.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.subcategory: directional efficacy predictions without empirical basis
issues.description: The authors make specific ordinal predictions about relative efficacy (Demonstration and motivation > Extended warning > Education about memory) despite acknowledging that no prior data exist to estimate effect sizes for these methods in this paradigm. These rank-order predictions are weakly justified ('tentatively assume') and risk being treated as confirmed hypotheses; given the power analysis cannot detect small effects, such fine-grained ordinal claims are not adequately supported by the design.
issues.quote: we tentatively assume that the most effective technique in reducing the memory conformity effect will be Demonstration and motivation... the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.subcategory: underpowered for planned subgroup and pairwise comparisons
issues.description: The chosen sample of 240 provides power only for medium-to-large effects in the omnibus interaction (medium requires 112; small requires 664). For the planned pairwise comparisons between two groups, a small effect requires 492 participants. Additionally, the proposed moderation analyses (efficacy higher among participants 'aware of discrepancies,' disputed vs non-disputed subsets) involve subgroups that will be substantially underpowered, yet these moderation hypotheses are central to the theoretical framework. The manuscript does not address power for these key subgroup/moderation tests.
issues.quote: a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

issues.subcategory: awareness-of-discrepancy moderation conflates measurement with manipulation
issues.description: A central theoretical claim is that the interventions will work specifically for participants 'aware of discrepancies.' However, awareness of discrepancies is not manipulated; it is a measured, post-hoc, possibly intervention-affected characteristic (the interventions themselves may change awareness). Comparing efficacy across aware vs unaware subgroups is therefore correlational and subject to selection/confounding, so it cannot cleanly test the proposed informational-influence mechanism. The analysis plan does not specify how awareness will be measured or how its endogeneity will be handled.
issues.quote: we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.

issues.subcategory: missing measurement and analysis plan for confidence ratings
issues.description: Participants rate subjective certainty (0–100%) for each answer, and confidence is theoretically central (the framework repeatedly invokes lack of confidence in own memory as a mechanism). However, the analysis plan does not specify how confidence data will be analyzed or used to test the proposed confidence-based mechanism. Collecting a key theoretical variable without a pre-specified analysis introduces analytic flexibility and leaves a central mechanism untested.
issues.quote: for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).

issues.subcategory: exploratory analysis without specified model
issues.description: The plan to use DRM results 'as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique' is labeled exploratory but is entirely unspecified (no model form, no predictors, no outcome, no correction). This open-ended analysis adds researcher degrees of freedom and is not clearly separated from confirmatory tests, which is a concern in a Registered Report context.
issues.quote: As an additional exploratory analysis, the results on the DRM procedure will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.

issues.subcategory: disputed/non-disputed coding creates unequal, self-selected cells
issues.description: The plan to categorize discussed items as 'disputed' vs 'non-disputed' based on whether partners disagreed during discussion creates post-hoc subgroups whose sizes are determined by participant behavior, not design. These subsets will vary in size across participants and conditions, are confounded with item difficulty and participant memory, and were not powered for. Treating them as an analytic factor without addressing their endogenous, unbalanced nature risks biased and underpowered comparisons.
issues.quote: if a pair of participants disagreed with each other and gave different answers during the discussion of a given item, their answers will be classified as disputed... if Participant A gave an answer... and Participant B agreed with it or did not give an answer it will be classified as “non-disputed”.

issues.subcategory: no specification of handling for unresolved/'both responses' and missing data
issues.description: The collaborative test allows documenting 'both responses' when participants cannot agree, and the individual test permits 'don't know' answers; but the analysis plan does not specify how these cases, or general missing data, will be handled in the ANOVA indices. Since indices are counts (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total), the treatment of non-responses materially affects results, yet no missing-data strategy is described.
issues.quote: If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented.

issues.subcategory: filler task durations inconsistently described
issues.description: The procedure specifies filler tasks of '15 minutes' (logic puzzles) and 'five minutes' (multiplication) at specific points, but these durations and the overall sequence are not reconciled with the stated total session length of about 60 minutes given the 6.5-minute movie, ~7-minute podcasts, DRM task, two tests, debriefing, and purpose-probe. While minor, the timing budget appears tight/unreconciled and could affect replicability and delay-interval comparability across conditions (e.g., the DRM condition imposes a longer pre-test interval than control).
issues.quote: After watching the video, the participants will be engaged in a filler task (solving logic puzzles) for 15 minutes.... the participants will be asked to work on multiplication problems for five minutes.... One experimental session will last about 60 minutes.

issues.subcategory: retention-interval confound between conditions
issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation condition includes an additional active DRM task plus feedback before the individual memory test, whereas other conditions only involve a ~7-minute podcast. This means the time between misinformation exposure and the final test, and the amount of intervening cognitive activity, differs systematically across conditions. Such differences in retention interval and interpolated activity are themselves known to affect memory and could confound any observed differences in efficacy.
issues.quote: Participants in the DRM group will be given the DRM procedure with feedback, described above, which usually results in most of the participants falsely recalling a few of the critical lures.
